components.text: The dating of traditions as early evidence independently supports proximity to the supposed historical person.
The decisive claim that the traditions are unusually early depends on locating them near the disputed Gospel-era chronology.
Legendary narrative shaping can coexist with the existence of the person around whom stories accumulate.
The decisive distinction is whether legendary molding can be removed while leaving an independently explanatory historical person.
Multiple early oral and written traditions provide independent attestation to an underlying Jesus.
The decisive demand is whether the purported sources independently attest Jesus rather than merely transmit Christian claims.
Multiple independent first-century traditions provide unusually early evidence for Jesus.
The decisive claim concerns multiple independent first-century traditions, while this reply isolates the authenticity of a later Josephus passage.
Q, M, L, and extracanonical traditions establish multiple independent sources predating the canonical Gospels.
The decisive demand is whether several asserted early sources are real, independent witnesses rather than products of a contested source model.
Paul describes an earthly Jewish teacher crucified by earthly opponents rather than a celestial figure.
The decisive demand is whether Paul's language locates Christ's death among earthly opponents or permits celestial demonic rulers.
Paul's sayings and characterization of Jesus constitute evidence of an earthly preacher and teacher.
The decisive demand is whether Pauline references to Jesus preserve earthly biography and teaching or derive from revelation.
Ancient external material only attests circulating Christian claims rather than an underlying earthly Jesus.
The decisive demand is whether non-Christian or hostile testimony merely repeats Christian claims or independently presupposes an earthly Jesus.
Removing miracles leaves mundane incidents with no adequate historical or explanatory core.
The decisive demand is whether critical analysis can recover historical claims despite disputed source reconstruction and miraculous narrative material.
Surviving Gnostic celestial-man materials provide a suitable background for interpreting Paul's letters.
The decisive support for the celestial Pauline model invokes surviving Gnostic materials as parallels or background.
A mundane teacher and incidents lack the causal power needed to generate Christianity.
The decisive earlier demand concerns whether Paul's execution scene is celestial and later historicized rather than earthly.
Later Gnostic writings cannot supply a first-century or earlier background for Pauline celestial concepts.
Christianity's exalted Christ requires resurrection belief arising around an executed historical teacher.
The decisive demand is whether a mythic divine-son background can plausibly predate Paul despite the late extant Gnostic texts.
An actual execution best explains why followers proclaimed a counterexpectational crucified Messiah.
Resurrection belief transforms an ordinary crucified teacher into the center of Christianity.
The decisive demand is whether an executed Jewish teacher plus resurrection belief adequately explains Christianity's emergence.
Critical historical methods can recover substantial claims about Jesus from individually evaluated traditions.
The decisive demand is whether a historical person existed behind the traditions, not merely whether reconstructions of his identity vary.
A mundane historical figure is inadequate because the relevant Christian figure is the miracle-working Christ.
Removing supernatural claims leaves no meaningful basis for retaining the existence of the underlying person.
The decisive demand is whether the gap between a mundane figure and miraculous stories undermines the underlying person's existence.
Whether false supernatural accretions can coexist with a historical person beneath the resulting tradition.
False miraculous traditions can surround an existing ordinary person without erasing that person's historicity.
The decisive issue is whether bare compatibility with existence supplies an adequate historical foundation for the exalted Christ tradition.
Whether a commonplace founder remains explanatorily significant after legendary accretions are distinguished from personal existence.
A legendary or miraculous biography remains compatible with a person securely located in ordinary history.
Critical analysis can remove defective traditions while recovering a substantial historically anchored core.
The decisive demand is whether Gospel traditions contain reliable contextual anchors rather than literary or historically defective placements.
Whether critical removal of defective narrative anchors still leaves a historically locatable and recoverable Jesus.
Defects in Gospel historical anchors leave Jesus free-floating and freely insertable into history.
Rival interpretive paradigms prevent confident historical conclusions from fragmentary evidence.
The decisive methodological demand is how fragmentary and paradigm-laden evidence can justify a historical existence judgment.
Whether remaining evidence retains comparative force when individual narrative anchors are challenged.
Whether multiple, proximate sources provide better evidence than late singular hearsay despite imperfect certainty.
